content:
Just so we're clear...inlining is where the functions present in the data file are linked to other stuff that hasn't been clearly identified yet, right?

Or is it **way** worse than I'm thinking?

author: Mrkol
content: na, inlining is where instead of actually calling a function the compiler instead slaps it's contents in the place where it's called

author: Mrkol
content: and then it sees that "oh, that function is not used anywhere, lets throw it out"

author: Mrkol
content: and then we get huuuuuuuuuge functions while the original source code had it all neatly organized into smaller functions

author: Flash
content: ...Wait...how the heck does that make any sense? The compiler shouldn't be able to make code work like that.

author: Mrkol
content: it is absoslutely allowed to inline stuff

author: Flash
content: Because obviously all the functions in the data file link back to the root of where it grabs its defined structs from...so it instead having the code itself there not being linked to anything when it *should* makes things hella confusing to track the origin of.

author: blu
blu
content: but sometimes it replaces it in a way that only happens with inlines (I think messing with register usage and stack size?)

author: vabold
content: non-volatile GPR usage is a pretty good indicator of inlines

author: vabold
vabold
content: code linking against that object *could* still call `f`, but if it doesn't, `f` isn't used by `g`, gets unused, and therefore gets stripped out of the final binary

author: Flash
content: ...So all it does is just make the code confusing to read for analysers, but the compiler says "Eh fuck it, if it works, it works."

author: vabold
content: the compiler does this because it's faster

author: Flash
content: OK, I suppose that makes more sense. The compiler would be aiming for optimisation, not readability.

author: Flash
content: Less wasted CPU cycles means more time running code before intercepts.

author: vabold
content: if g called f normally, you'd have to make a stack frame for both g and f. if g doesn't call f normally and instead embeds it, it can make the stack frame for both at once

author: vabold
vabold
content: incidentally I'm dealing with this exact problem now trying to work out what's happening with nw4r math types

author: vabold
content: and yes, it's exhausting trying to track down specs that only half exist

author: Flash
content:
...So let me try to summarize the whole problem.

The compiler inlines code because it is efficent, but inlining code strips it away of valuable information for tracking down where the origin of values/structs come from. Thus its really only through trial and error that you have to unravel the code itself to identify if your restored function matches what the compiler would've optimised otherwise.

TL;DR, compiler shrinks code for speed, code is hard to read, trying to decompile takes effort to restore it back to the OG source code.

Is that a correct way of perceiving it?

author: vabold
content: it's less tracking down the origin of values/structs and more tracking the origin of variables, but yeah

author: vabold
content: as a more practical example of how inlining can screw you over, this was a scratch sent in <#873250400483024976> (<https://decomp.me/scratch/geDpo>), and this was the solution: <https://decomp.me/scratch/hHWwq>

author: vabold
content: non-volatile GPRs are ordered based on what their "cost" is, i.e. "how much effort would it be to restore the original variable if it leaked"

author: vabold
content: this cullMode variable was getting put in r28, but the cost needed to increase while everything else stayed relatively the same

author: vabold
content: when you don't account for the inline, the cost is lowered because it can in theory just be inferred from the direction

author: vabold
content: but when inlining a function with it as an argument, the cost becomes much higher because the compiler now can't afford to leak it. it's a hard requirement for this function to work, regardless of if the function was inlined

content: Yeesh. It's a lot more in-depth than I'm grasping here.

author: Flash

content: it's a very big problem and there's a million different ways inlining can affect codegen

content:
```Yes—the core claim is proven independently of linker dead-stripping.

Controlled builds changed only -prefix SMS.mch:

Retail function    No-PCH vs retail    PCH vs retail

TSpcInterp::update    Exact, identical SHA-256    276 differing bytes
ReInitTransform    Exact, identical SHA-256    4 differing bytes


The linker cannot explain this: dead-stripping may remove unused PCH literals, but it cannot alter already-compiled function bodies. Therefore these retail translation units exhibit no-PCH compilation behavior, proving that applying the PCH indiscriminately to every game unit is incorrect.

RumbleData supports the conclusion—PCH adds 40 bytes absent from retail—but Mrkol’s dead-stripping objection is plausible for data alone. The two exact function comparisons close that loophole.

I cannot substantiate the specific “regressed to 7%” number from the retained builds. The reproducible regressions were 100% → 99.26% and 100% → 99.97%.

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="48217"} I proved it using function bodies, so linker dead-stripping can’t explain the result.

I compiled the same sources with identical MWCC flags, changing only whether -prefix SMS.mch was present:

TSpcInterp::update: retail and no-PCH are byte-for-byte identical; PCH differs in 276 bytes.

ReInitTransform: retail and no-PCH are byte-for-byte identical; PCH differs in 4 bytes.


Dead-stripping can remove unused PCH data symbols during linking, but it cannot rewrite a function compiled with the PCH into the exact no-PCH machine code. So at least these retail TUs were compiled with no-PCH behavior, and applying the PCH blindly to every game object is demonstrably wrong.

I can’t reproduce my earlier “around 7%” number from the retained builds, so I’m withdrawing that specific figure. The underlying claim is still proven. :::```
